newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH DRIVERS HIT BY RECENT GASOLINE, DOLLAR SURGE.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH DRIVERS HIT BY RECENT GASOLINE, DOLLAR SURGE.

text.p: Dutch drivers will face petrol pump prices some 12 percent higher than a month ago as both the dollar and gasoline market prices have soared.
Gasoline prices at the pump are also 28 percent higher than this time last year.
The latest rises in the recommended retail prices by Shell, scheduled to take effect on Friday, led the oil giant to include an explanation of the recent price hikes.
"We felt it is important for our customers to know why the prices are going up," Shell said.

The price hike came the day benchmark gasoline prices in the Rotterdam market hit their highest level since the Gulf War, $240 a tonne, and the dollar touched 2.13 Dutch guilders, its highest level since October 1989.
"The figures emphasise that the recent price rises are entirely market driven and as market conditions allow prices will spring back," Shell said.
The Dutch are of course not unique among consumers in continental Europe, all suffering from the combined effect of high gasoline prices and the strong dollar.
However, the Dutch were confronted with a 13 cent rise in petrol duty to 1.29 guilders on July 1 and, some observers argue, service station competition is not as keen as in other European countries.
In March, the Dutch government launched an inquiry into why pump prices were so much higher than in neighbouring countries.
In Germany, for example, petrol prices have risen over five percent in the past month, the average price of unleaded premium standing at 1.70 marks per litre.
"The price rises every two weeks by, say, four pfennigs, but competition in the market starts and the prices gradually fall," said a spokesman at German service station group Aral.
